title: Czech culture and traditions
summary: Everyday customs at work and at home, the history behind them, all 13 public holidays and the traditions around Christmas and Easter, with phrases to practise.

phrases.en: Merry Christmas!
phrases.note: Vánoce is plural, so the adjective is plural too: veselé.

phrases.en: Happy holidays!
phrases.note: Common in cards and e-mails to colleagues in December.

phrases.en: Happy New Year!

phrases.cs: Veselé Vánoce a šťastný nový rok!
phrases.en: Merry Christmas and a happy New Year!

phrases.cs: Hodně zdraví a štěstí v novém roce!
phrases.en: Lots of health and happiness in the new year!
What did you get for Christmas? (lit. What did the baby Jesus bring you?)

phrases.cs: Na Štědrý den jíme kapra a bramborový salát.
phrases.en: On Christmas Eve we eat carp and potato salad.
Are you baking Christmas biscuits?
Happy New Year 2027 (on cards)
phrases.note: From French "pour féliciter". Seen on cards and in e-mail signatures in December and January.

phrases.en: Happy Easter!

phrases.cs: Hody, hody, doprovody, dejte vejce malovaný.
phrases.en: Hey, hey, give us a painted egg. (Easter Monday rhyme)
phrases.note: Traditional rhyme, in dialect form (malovaný for malované).

phrases.en: Where will you be for Easter?
phrases.note: o + locative plural: o Velikonocích, o Vánocích.

phrases.en: We're going to the witch-burning (30 April).
A kiss under a blossoming cherry tree! (1 May)
Happy birthday!
phrases.note: k + dative plural: narozeniny → k narozeninám.

phrases.en: Happy name day!
When is your name day?

phrases.cs: Dneska mám svátek, dejte si dort.
phrases.en: It's my name day today, have some cake.
Cheers!
phrases.note: Look each person in the eye as you clink glasses.

phrases.en: To you! (a toast to the person celebrating)

phrases.cs: Zítra je svátek, obchody jsou zavřené.
phrases.en: Tomorrow is a public holiday; the shops are closed.
We've got a long weekend.
Are you going to the cottage?
Where are you going for the long weekend?

phrases.cs: Ve čtvrtek je státní svátek, v pátek si beru volno.
phrases.en: Thursday is a public holiday; I'm taking Friday off.

practice.title: Christmas and New Year
practice.description: Wishes, customs and the grammar inside them.

exercises.prompt: Merry Christmas!
exercises.why: Veselé Vánoce! Vánoce is a plural word, so the adjective is plural: veselé.

exercises.prompt: Happy New Year!
exercises.why: Šťastný nový rok! (rok is masculine inanimate, so in the accusative of a wish it stays the same).

exercises.prompt: Přeju vám vesel___ Vánoce.
exercises.en: I wish you a merry Christmas.
exercises.why: Vánoce is plural, so adjectives describing it are plural: veselé Vánoce.

hints.explain: Vánoce is plural. Standard Czech is veselé (you will hear veselý in casual speech).
Vánoce is plural, not feminine singular: veselé Vánoce.

exercises.prompt: Co ti přinesl Ježíšek?
answers: What did {baby Jesus|the baby Jesus|Ježíšek|Jesus|little Jesus|the Christ Child|Santa|Father Christmas} bring you[?]
What did you get for Christmas[?]
exercises.why: In Czech homes, presents are brought by Ježíšek, the baby Jesus, on Christmas Eve.

exercises.prompt: What fish do most Czech families eat for Christmas Eve dinner? Type the Czech word.
exercises.why: kapr (carp), usually fried, with potato salad. Live carp are sold from tubs in the street before Christmas.

hints.explain: Right fish: now the Czech word, kapr.

exercises.prompt: What does **PF** stand for on a Czech New Year card?

hints.explain: Post festum is Latin for "after the party": too late. PF is French: pour féliciter.
Nothing to do with Prague: PF is French, pour féliciter, "to congratulate".

exercises.why: PF = pour féliciter (French, "to congratulate"): PF 2027 means "Happy New Year 2027".

exercises.prompt: Wish her the same, and a happy New Year (you say vy to her).
answers: [{Děkuju|Děkuji|Díky}[,] ]{Vám {taky|také}|{Veselé|Krásné} Vánoce i vám}[,] a šťastný nový rok[!]
exercises.why: Vám taky (you too) or Veselé Vánoce i vám, then a šťastný nový rok.

hints.wrong: [{Děkuju|Děkuji|Díky}[,] ]{Tobě {taky|také}|{Veselé|Krásné} Vánoce i tobě}[,] a šťastný nový rok[!]
hints.explain: You say vy to her, so: vám taky, not tobě.

practice.title: Easter and spring
practice.description: Easter wishes and the spring customs.

exercises.prompt: Happy Easter!
exercises.why: Veselé Velikonoce! Velikonoce is plural, like Vánoce.

exercises.prompt: What is the braided willow whip used on Easter Monday called? Type the Czech word.
exercises.why: pomlázka: boys and men use it for a light, symbolic swat "for health and youth", and get painted eggs in return.

exercises.prompt: What are decorated Easter eggs called? Type the Czech word.
exercises.why: kraslice: decorated eggs, given to the boys who come round with the pomlázka.

exercises.prompt: What do Czechs "burn" on bonfires on the night of 30 April? Type the Czech word.
exercises.why: čarodějnice (witches): pálení čarodějnic, "the burning of the witches", usually a straw figure on the bonfire.

hints.explain: Right idea: now in Czech, čarodějnice.

exercises.prompt: O Velikonoc___ jedu domů.
exercises.why: o + locative. Velikonoce is plural, and the locative plural ends in -ích: o Velikonocích (at Easter), o Vánocích (at Christmas).

hints.explain: After o (at a time), use the locative plural: o Velikonocích.

exercises.prompt: O Vánoc___ jsme vždycky doma.
exercises.en: We're always at home at Christmas.
exercises.why: o + locative plural: o Vánocích (at Christmas).

hints.explain: After o (at a time), use the locative plural: o Vánocích.

practice.title: Name days, birthdays and toasts
practice.description: What to say when a colleague celebrates.

exercises.prompt: Happy birthday!
exercises.why: Všechno nejlepší k narozeninám: "all the best for (your) birthday". k + dative plural: narozeniny → k narozeninám.

hints.explain: k (for, towards) takes the dative: k narozeninám.

exercises.prompt: Happy name day!
exercises.why: Všechno nejlepší k svátku (or ke svátku). svátek means both "name day" and "public holiday".

hints.explain: k takes the dative: k svátku.

exercises.prompt: Cheers!
exercises.why: Na zdraví! (to health). Look each person in the eye as you clink glasses.

exercises.prompt: When is your name day? (informal)
exercises.why: Kdy máš svátek? (or jmeniny). svátek = name day.

exercises.prompt: On your birthday or name day at a Czech office, who usually brings the cake or snacks?

hints.explain: In Czechia it's the other way round: the person celebrating brings the treat, and colleagues congratulate them.
Not the boss: the person celebrating brings the cake, biscuits or chlebíčky.

exercises.why: The person celebrating brings the treat (cake, biscuits, chlebíčky), and colleagues congratulate them.

context.speaker: Kolegyně
context.cs: Dneska mám svátek, dejte si dort!
context.en: It's my name day today, have some cake!

exercises.prompt: Wish her a happy name day.
exercises.why: Všechno nejlepší k svátku!

hints.explain: It's her name day (svátek), not her birthday: Všechno nejlepší k svátku!

practice.title: Public holidays and history
practice.description: The dates your colleagues take off, and why.

exercises.prompt: Which date is the anniversary of the Velvet Revolution, now a public holiday?

hints.explain: 28 October is the founding of Czechoslovakia (1918). The Velvet Revolution began on 17 November 1989.
1 January is New Year's Day and the restoration of the independent Czech state (1993).

exercises.why: 17 November: Struggle for Freedom and Democracy Day, remembering the student protests of 1939 and 1989.

exercises.prompt: Czechoslovakia was founded on 28 October of which year?

hints.explain: 1938 is the year of the Munich Agreement. Czechoslovakia was founded twenty years earlier.
1968 is the Prague Spring and the invasion that ended it.
1993 is when Czechoslovakia split into Czechia and Slovakia. It was founded in 1918.

exercises.why: 28 October 1918, after the collapse of Austria-Hungary. Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk became the first president.

exercises.prompt: Which saint, the patron of the Czech lands, is remembered on 28 September?

hints.explain: St Vitus gives his name to the cathedral at Prague Castle, but 28 September is St Wenceslas.
Jan Hus is remembered on 6 July.

exercises.why: 28 September is St Wenceslas (svatý Václav), now Czech Statehood Day. Wenceslas Square is named after him.

exercises.prompt: Which religious reformer, burned at the stake in 1415, is remembered on 6 July?

hints.explain: Žižka was the Hussite general in the wars that followed Hus's death.
Masaryk was the first president of Czechoslovakia, in 1918.

exercises.why: Jan Hus preached in Czech and challenged the Church; his death led to the Hussite wars.

exercises.prompt: Zítra je svátek, obchody jsou zavřené.
exercises.why: svátek here means a public holiday; zavřené = closed (plural, agreeing with obchody).

exercises.prompt: We've got a long weekend.
exercises.why: prodloužený víkend = "extended weekend". víkend is masculine inanimate, so the accusative is unchanged.

hints.explain: Understandable, but Czechs say prodloužený víkend (extended weekend).

exercises.prompt: The Munich Agreement of 1938 is often summed up in four Czech words meaning "about us, without us". Type them.
exercises.why: O nás bez nás: Czechoslovakia was not invited to the conference that gave its border regions to Nazi Germany.

timeline.title: Cyril and Methodius arrive
timeline.summary: Two Byzantine missionaries come to Great Moravia, bringing Christianity and the first Slavic alphabet.
timeline.significance: The start of written Slavic culture. Their feast day, 5 July, is a public holiday, which is why July often begins with a long weekend.
timeline.place: Their statue on Charles Bridge, and the Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius in Resslova street.

timeline.title: Saint Wenceslas
timeline.summary: Duke Wenceslas (Václav) is murdered by his brother, in 929 or 935, and soon venerated as a saint.
timeline.significance: The "eternal prince" and patron of the Czech lands. Legend says knights sleep inside Blaník hill, ready to wake when the nation is in danger. 28 September is Czech Statehood Day.
timeline.place: The equestrian statue at the top of Wenceslas Square, the classic place to meet: "pod koněm" (under the horse).

timeline.title: Charles IV and the golden age
timeline.summary: The King of Bohemia, later Holy Roman Emperor, makes Prague an imperial capital: Charles University (1348), the New Town, Charles Bridge (1357).
timeline.significance: Much of the Prague visitors admire is his. In a 2005 national TV poll, Czechs voted him the greatest Czech of all time.
timeline.place: Charles Bridge, the Karolinum (the university's oldest building) and the New Town around Karlovo náměstí.

timeline.title: Jan Hus burned at the stake
timeline.summary: The reformer who preached in Czech and criticised the Church is burned at the Council of Konstanz. The Hussite wars follow.
timeline.significance: A symbol of conscience and of the Czech language: Hus is traditionally credited with the háček and čárka. His motto "Pravda vítězí" (Truth prevails) is on the presidential flag. 6 July is a public holiday.
timeline.place: The Hus monument on Old Town Square and the Bethlehem Chapel (Betlémská kaple), where he preached.

timeline.title: The Battle of White Mountain
timeline.summary: The Protestant Czech estates are defeated. In 1621, 27 of their leaders are executed on Old Town Square.
timeline.significance: Remembered as the beginning of the "dark age" (temno): three centuries of Habsburg rule, forced re-Catholicisation and the exile of thinkers such as Jan Amos Komenský (Comenius).
timeline.place: 27 white crosses in the pavement by the Old Town Hall; the battlefield memorial at Bílá Hora, the terminus of tram 22.

timeline.title: The National Revival
timeline.summary: Writers and scholars bring Czech back as a language of literature, science and the stage. The National Theatre opens in 1883, paid for by public collections.
timeline.significance: Without it, Czech might have survived only as a rural dialect. It's why the language is cherished, why Czech coined its own words for many things, and why Czechs light up when foreigners learn it.
timeline.place: "Národ sobě" (The nation to itself) in gold above the stage of the National Theatre; the National Museum at the top of Wenceslas Square.

timeline.title: Czechoslovakia is born
timeline.summary: On 28 October, as Austria-Hungary collapses, an independent Czechoslovakia is declared. Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk becomes its first president.
timeline.significance: A modern democracy in the heart of Europe, and the reason 28 October is the main national holiday. Masaryk is still the model of a principled president.
timeline.place: The Municipal House (Obecní dům), where independence was proclaimed, and the Masaryk statue by Prague Castle.

timeline.title: The Munich Agreement
timeline.summary: Britain, France, Germany and Italy agree to hand the Czech border regions to Nazi Germany, without Czechoslovakia at the table.
timeline.significance: "O nás bez nás", about us, without us: still shorthand for great powers deciding Czech fate, and a source of lasting scepticism.

timeline.title: Occupation and resistance
timeline.summary: German troops occupy Prague in March 1939. On 17 November 1939 the Nazis close Czech universities after student protests. In 1942, Czechoslovak paratroopers assassinate Reinhard Heydrich; the village of Lidice is destroyed in revenge.
timeline.significance: 17 November became International Students' Day. Operation Anthropoid is one of the most famous resistance acts of the war, and Lidice is remembered worldwide.
timeline.place: The crypt of the Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius in Resslova street, where the paratroopers made their last stand, with bullet marks still in the wall.

timeline.title: Uprising and liberation
timeline.summary: Prague rises against the occupiers on 5 May; the war in Europe ends days later.
timeline.significance: 8 May, Victory Day, is a public holiday. Small plaques remembering those who fell in the uprising are on buildings all over the city, often with fresh flowers.
timeline.place: The Czech Radio building on Vinohradská street, scene of heavy fighting in 1945 (and again in 1968).

timeline.title: The communist takeover
timeline.summary: In February the Communist Party seizes power. Forty-one years of one-party rule begin.
timeline.significance: This period shaped your colleagues' parents and grandparents: closed borders, nationalised companies, and the panelák housing estates you still see on the edges of every city.
timeline.place: The vast panelák estate of Jižní Město, around Háje and Opatov on metro line C.

timeline.title: Prague Spring and invasion
timeline.summary: Alexander Dubček's attempt at "socialism with a human face" is crushed when Warsaw Pact armies invade on the night of 20–21 August.
timeline.significance: Remembered every 21 August, and one reason many Czechs have strong feelings about Russia. "Normalisation" followed: two decades of grey conformity.
timeline.place: Wenceslas Square and the Czech Radio building, where Praguers faced the tanks.

timeline.title: Jan Palach
timeline.summary: In January, the student Jan Palach sets himself on fire on Wenceslas Square in protest against the nation's resignation after the invasion.
timeline.significance: A lasting symbol of resistance through conscience. Students and politicians still lay flowers at his memorial each January.
timeline.place: The memorial in the pavement in front of the National Museum, Jan Palach Square (náměstí Jana Palacha) by the Rudolfinum, and his grave at Olšany Cemetery (metro Želivského).

timeline.title: Charter 77
timeline.summary: Dissidents, including the playwright Václav Havel, sign a document demanding that the regime respect human rights.
timeline.significance: It built the network of dissidents who led the 1989 revolution; many signatories became the new country's leaders.

timeline.title: The Velvet Revolution
timeline.summary: Police beat a peaceful student march on Národní třída. Within weeks, mass protests and a general strike bring down the regime; Václav Havel becomes president.
timeline.significance: A peaceful revolution and a point of national pride. 17 November is a public holiday. Havel's line "Pravda a láska musí zvítězit nad lží a nenávistí" (Truth and love must prevail over lies and hatred) is still quoted.
timeline.place: The bronze hands memorial in the arcade on Národní třída, where people light candles every 17 November, and the balcony on Wenceslas Square from which Havel and Dubček spoke.

timeline.title: The Velvet Divorce
timeline.summary: Czechoslovakia splits peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia.
timeline.significance: The two nations remain close: most Czechs understand Slovak, and Slovak TV, music and colleagues are everywhere. 1 January is the restoration of the independent Czech state.

timeline.title: NATO and the European Union
timeline.summary: Czechia joins NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.
timeline.significance: The freedom to live and work across Europe, which is part of why so many international companies, and you, are here.
